title: 'The Otherworld Is Home' Explores Personal Reclamation, Cultural Identity, and Spiritual Passage
description: The Haggerty Museum of Art at Marquette University hosts free-to-the-public exhibitions and programs inviting a journey across multiple centuries
body:
The Haggerty Museum of Art at Marquette University hosts free-to-the-public exhibitions and programs inviting a journey across multiple centuries and continents titled The Otherworld is Home. Inspired by the Yorùbá proverb, “Life is a journey, the otherworld is home” (ayé l’àjò, ọ̀run n’ilé), the museum-wide presentation explores themes of personal reclamation, cultural identity, spiritual passage, and connection across Africa’s many diasporas.
The three simultaneous exhibitions below offer opportunities to explore the enduring resonance of African artistic traditions and their continued influence on contemporary life. These exhibitions are activated with a full slate of programming that may be found on the museum’s events page.

African Art: Ancient Roots, Enduring Values
Featuring more than 40 classical and neoclassical works, this exhibition highlights how African artists use traditional craftsmanship to connect the tangible and spiritual worlds. “This exhibition and essay explore how, what, and why African works of art . . . work: how they move and affect us; what roles they perform; and the ways they may acquire different purposes, meanings, and values as they travel across oceans and cultural, political, and religious boundaries over time and space,” writes guest curator and scholar of African and African diaspora arts Henry John Drewal.

Iké Udé: Sartorial Anarchy
Artist Iké Udé’s ongoing photographic series Sartorial Anarchy merges clothing and objects from different times and places to upend recognizable signifiers of cultural and individual identity. The Nigerian born artist, now living in New York City, transforms himself into a multifaceted amalgam of many identities in these photographic self-portraits. According to the artist, “In each image, I married disparate costumes from widely diverse traditions, countries, and time frames. And in mixing eras and cultures, I was able to bring harmony, as it were, to their similarly irreconcilable differences.”

Thresholds
Thresholds brings together the work of Aisha Tandiwe Bell, Portia Cobb, Stephen Hamilton, and Daniel Minter to dynamically explore the depth, complexity, and resilience of Black cultural memory. The artists create at a threshold between the seen and unseen, the present and the ancestral, and the place left behind and the place arrived at. Working across several media, they present their work alongside African works from the Haggerty’s collection to create a “call and response,” a participatory exchange in which one voice calls out and others answer in turn. Building on a shared yet continually unfolding cultural memory, where the past remains active and unresolved, these practices become sites of inspiration, critical reflection, and renewal.
To learn more, visit marquette.edu/haggerty-museum.

title: Edge-to-Edge Splendor Fills Maria Yolanda Liebana's Buoyant Paintings
description: Tarot, pop culture, and personal narrative converge in the maximalist, mixed-media paintings of Maria Yolanda Liebana. The New York-based artist o
body:
Tarot, pop culture, and personal narrative converge in the maximalist, mixed-media paintings of Maria Yolanda Liebana. The New York-based artist opens her first institutional solo exhibition at Montclair State University’s George Segal Gallery this month.
Titled A Place to Be Held, Liebana’s show revolves around a fantastical, Eden-like garden exploding with an extravaganza of rainbows, flowers, clouds, cosmic phenomena, and more. “The exhibition imagines a matriarchal world where chance, identity, and desire are always in motion,” says a statement.
“The Aleph’s Seduction” (2024)
Liebana incorporates a wide range of materials into her vibrant works, including wallpaper, mirror tiles, pearls, glitter, disco balls, sequins, and rhinestones. She embraces the luminosity of joy and playfulness while nodding to Catholicism and ancient mythologies, invoked by symbols like chalices and cherubs.
As a first-generation Latinx immigrant who grew up in New Jersey, the artist has long been interested in the nature of selfhood and inheritance, and the birth of her daughter inspired a body of work that explores motherhood “as both a physical and spiritual terrain shaped by labor, wonder, and transformation.” She depicts confident, empowered women who dance, recline, and enjoy one another’s company, representing universal feminine dominion and strength.
A Place to Be Held opens on September 15 and continues through December 11 in Montclair, New Jersey. See more on the artist’s Instagram.

title: Henry Wessel's Candid California Photos Underscore the Art of Noticing
description: “There is the world, and there is the photograph. The photograph is not the world, it’s a completely different thing,” Henry Wessel (1942-2018) sa
body:
“There is the world, and there is the photograph. The photograph is not the world, it’s a completely different thing,” Henry Wessel (1942-2018) said in a “TateShots” short on the occasion of Tate Modern’s display of his Incidents series in 2014. Today, an exhibition of more than 65 prints titled Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books opens at The Grolier Club, a historic society celebrating the world of books and the graphic arts.
Wessel was a New Jersey native who, after borrowing a Leica camera during his studies at Pennsylvania State University, fell headlong into photography. He rose to prominence in the early 1970s for his black-and-white compositions that plumbed the possibilities of landscape and documentary imagery. Following the receipt of a Guggenheim grant, he moved to the Bay Area, where he taught at the now-defunct San Francisco Art Institute from 1973 to 2014 and captured the area’s characteristically glowing light, historic neighborhoods, and individualistic denizens.
“Untitled” (1968), gelatin silver print
Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes the artist’s Incidents and Traffic series in their totality, plus works from his Real Estate and Night Walks series. To make the latter, he would walk around neighborhoods with his tripod and take portraits of local homes after dinner or during the early morning hours.
In Traffic, Wessel snapped scenes and other drivers from his car, capturing candid moments as other vehicles passed or as he encountered roadside curiosities. But he quickly learned that there’s an inherent issue with having to stop the car, get out, and try to capture what you initially saw: it looks totally different.
Wessel began to capture what he saw directly from the driver’s seat, working quickly with the hope that the images would more closely translate his immediate experiences. In an SFMOMA interview he said, “You know, like they say, luck is impartial. You have just as much bad luck as you have good luck. But you can do things to prepare yourself to receive the good luck. And that’s part of the whole process of photographing.”
Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes some of Wessel’s earliest work, such as “Untitled” from 1968, plus the other series that were created throughout the 1980s and 1990s. The show opens today and continues through November 14 in New York, and a catalogue slated for release in October is available for pre-order from Chicago University Press.

title: Spanning 200+ Works, a New Book Celebrates the World of Fungi
description: Following surveys of butterflies, birds, oceans, and trees, the editors at Phaidon have settled on their next topic of inquiry: fungi. This Octobe
body:
Following surveys of butterflies, birds, oceans, and trees, the editors at Phaidon have settled on their next topic of inquiry: fungi. This October, the publisher will release an expansive tome gathering more than 200 photographs, artworks, historical objects, and more all devoted to the vast diversity and creative potential of mycology.
Fungi: The World of Mushrooms spans more than 200 pages and several millennia, compiling a breadth of imagery from ancient history to the present day. Included are the uncanny costumes shot in-situ by Riitta Ikonen and Anni Koponen, Hima af Klint’s delicate illustrations, and Carsten Höller’s disorienting installation of suspended toadstools.
Fungi is slated for release on October 15, and you can reserve your copy in the Colossal Shop.

title: Could a Kid Do It? The Wa Transforms Buildings into Childlike Drawings
description: Although there’s no official count, the amount of World War II bunkers, battery platforms, and other structures found along European coastlines pr
body:
Although there’s no official count, the amount of World War II bunkers, battery platforms, and other structures found along European coastlines probably number in the tens of thousands. The structures were typically made of concrete, and many are located along what’s known as the Atlantic Wall, an extensive coastal network of defenses built by the Nazis between 1942 and 1944 in anticipation of attacks by Allied forces. Disused now for decades, they’re a blight on the landscape, but one that The Wa sees as a blank canvas for something much more playful and bright.
In his series A Kid Could Do It, The Wa transforms otherwise nondescript structures into jubilantly youthful drawings, literally scribbling in saturated colors and adding blocky windows, doors, and flowers. The title of the project, of course, will sound familiar to any artist working in abstraction or museum-goer who has stood looking at a Jackson Pollock or Franz Kline painting and heard someone nearby murmur derisively, “My kid could do that.”

The Wa turns the table on this sentiment, including in a large-scale rendition on an empty house in Stuttgart as part of this year’s PFFFestival. We encounter windows with purple curtains in seemingly random places, a door that’s narrower on the bottom than the top, a roof with scalloped shapes that could be shingles or clouds, and of course, huge scrawls of bright blue and red.
For PFFFestival, as with his earlier bunker paintings, the artist follows what he describes as “one simple rule: the unfiltered creative logic of a child.” A Kid Could Do It also nods to the collaborative nature of how the project began, as The Wa started the series by working alongside his mother. In a manner of speaking, a kid really did do it.
See more on The Wa’s Instagram.

title: Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch Steps Down Amid Trump’s Attacks
description:
News
                “​​I leave with pride and sadness,” said the institution’s secretary, pledging to continue fighting to “pro
body:
News
                “​​I leave with pride and sadness,” said the institution’s secretary, pledging to continue fighting to “protect the integrity of the Smithsonian.”
            
                
                                
                            
                            
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch (photo Michael Hickey/Getty Images)
    
        
            Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch will step down from his post by the end of the year, amid ongoing attacks on the institution by President Donald Trump and his administration.In a statement shared with Hyperallergic, Bunch announced his departure with “very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude.”“There is no place like the Smithsonian — it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together,” Bunch said. “I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” Bunch was named the Smithsonian’s 14th secretary in June 2019, becoming the first Black American and first historian at the helm of the institution. He was previously the founding director of the African American History and Culture Museum, and had worked as a curator at the American History Museum and an education specialist at the National Air and Space Museum earlier in his career, totaling more than three decades of service at the Smithsonian. (Bunch also led the Chicago History Museum, a non-Smithsonian organization, from 2000 to 2005.) Since taking office in 2025, the Trump administration has sought to whitewash United States history by targeting the Smithsonian’s curatorial approaches, accusing the museum and research network of focusing too much on “how bad slavery was” and mandating essentialist concepts of gender.

title: Apply for a 2027–2028 Fellowship at the Smithsonian American Art Museum
description:
Announcement
                Fellowships at SAAM and its Renwick Gallery provide scholars with access to collections, community, and
body:
Announcement
                Fellowships at SAAM and its Renwick Gallery provide scholars with access to collections, community, and professional advancement.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            (Credit: Photo by Norwood Photography)
    
        
            The Smithsonian American Art Museum (SAAM) and its Renwick Gallery invite applications to its premier fellowship program, the oldest and largest in American art. Scholars from any discipline whose research engages the art, craft, and visual culture of the United States are encouraged to apply, as are those who foreground new perspectives, materials, and methodologies. Fellowships are residential and support full-time research in the Smithsonian collections. SAAM is devoted to advancing excellence in art history and encourages candidates from all backgrounds to apply.  ResourcesEach fellow is provided a carrel in SAAM’s Research and Scholars Center. There, they have access to the museum’s collection of over 47,600 works, specialized study collections and databases, the Smithsonian’s Archives of American Art, and an 180,000-volume branch library specializing in American art. The Research and Scholars Center is a short walk from other Smithsonian museums and libraries, the Library of Congress, the National Archives, and the National Gallery of Art. Regular workshops, seminars, and lectures provide a forum for lively scholarly exchange and professional advancement.Fellowships AvailableCandidates may apply to one or more of the following three opportunities:SIFP Fellowships at SAAM: SAAM hosts fellows through the Smithsonian Institution Fellowship Program (SIFP) and awards a number of named fellowships to predoctoral, postdoctoral, and senior candidates from this general pool. Deadline: October 15, 2026The Betsy James Wyeth Fellowship in Native American Art: This joint fellowship at SAAM and the National Museum of the American Indian is awarded for a twelve-month term at the predoctoral level or a nine-month term at the postdoctoral or senior level. Deadline: October 15, 2026The Audrey Flack Short-Term Fellowship: One fellowship is awarded annually at the predoctoral, postdoctoral, or senior level for a one-month term. Deadline: February 1, 2027For more information, visit americanart.si.edu/fellowships or email saamfellowships@si.edu.
